title: Common DNS Operational and Configuration Errors
summary: Describes errors often found in the way DNS servers are operated and configured, and in the data they contain. It is a practical checklist of mistakes to avoid. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The DNS is the Internet's phone book, and its records are easy to get wrong. This memo lists the mistakes that people who run name servers keep making, and gives the correct way to write the records. It is a checklist written in 1996, not a protocol specification.

subtitle: The mistakes that break DNS most often, and what to write in the zone file instead.

tldr.problem: Running a name server and filling it with zone data has many ways to go wrong, and the mistakes cost working services and mail.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through the common errors in zone data (PTR and A records, SOA timers, glue, CNAME, MX, wildcards, delegation) and in the day-to-day running of BIND, and says what to do instead.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1912 is an Informational memo, not a standard. It replaces RFC 1537 and records DNS requirements and common practice as of 1996.

today: RFC 1912 is an Informational memo and is not listed as obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It replaces RFC 1537 and remains a description of DNS requirements and common practice as they stood in 1996.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Running a nameserver is not a trivial task. Many decisions have to be made about what data to put in the DNS and how to set up servers, and many things can go wrong. The memo tries to address the common mistakes and pitfalls found both in the zone data a nameserver loads into memory and in the way the server itself is operated.

It also tries to summarize current Internet requirements and common practice, and to expand on issues raised in RFC 1537. The memo also touches on server and resolver bugs and on a few political issues in the way DNS is operated on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's phone book is easy to fill with wrong entries. This memo lists the mistakes people make when they set up a name server or write its records, so that others can avoid them.

sections.title: Names, Addresses and Reverse Records
sections.content:
Every Internet-reachable host should have a name, and many Internet services will not talk to a host that is not correctly registered in the DNS. For every IP address there should be a matching PTR record in the in-addr.arpa domain, and a multi-homed host, one with more than one IP address, needs a PTR record for each address and not only for the first. A PTR record must point back to a valid A record and not to an alias defined by a CNAME. When the two sets of records do not match, the result is a loss of Internet services similar to not being registered in the DNS at all.

DNS domain names consist of labels separated by single dots. A label used as a host name may contain only ASCII letters, digits and the '-' character. A label may start with a digit, as in 3com.com, but may not be all digits, and it must begin and end with a letter or a digit. Labels used for mail may contain any ASCII character except the so-called specials, the control characters and whitespace; the specials are the parentheses, angle brackets, at sign, comma, semicolon, colon, backslash, quotation mark, square brackets and period. Because almost every mail name on the Internet is also a host name, mail software should be liberal and accept the relaxed form.

Two further traps deserve attention. A name that is also a valid alternate syntax for the inet_ntoa() library call can be misread: typing 'telnet 0xe' would try to connect to IP address 0.0.0.14. And many resource records take more than one argument, so HINFO and RP need two; if one is missing, a server may return garbage for the missing field.
sections.plainLanguage: Every reachable computer needs a name, and the name must point back to its address. Check both directions: a record for the address, and a reverse record that leads back to a real address record and not to an alias.

sections.title: The SOA Record and Its Timers
sections.content:
The SOA record of every zone should carry the e-mail address of the person who maintains the DNS at that site, commonly called the hostmaster. The '@' in the address must be replaced by a '.' and the '.' in the local part, as in John.Smith@widget.xx, must be quoted with a preceding backslash. The RFC prefers the generic name hostmaster with a mail alias to redirect it, because the address has to reach real people: it is often used to report bad DNS data or to report security incidents.

Serial numbers need care. Even where a server accepts a decimal serial number, it is converted internally to an unsigned 32-bit integer, so a decimal serial can be incremented into a value that is numerically larger yet converts to a lower serial number. Decimal serial numbers have been officially deprecated in recent versions of BIND. The recommended syntax is YYYYMMDDnn, where nn is a revision number for the same day, and it will not overflow until the year 4294.

The four timers in the SOA record are written in seconds in the zone data. Refresh says how often a secondary polls the primary for a newer serial number, and can be as short as 20 minutes to 2 hours, or 2 to 12 hours when the Internet connection is slow or is started on demand. Retry says how long a secondary waits before trying the primary again, and is typically some fraction of the refresh interval. Expire says how long a secondary keeps treating its copy as valid without reaching the primary, and 2-4 weeks are suggested. Minimum is the default time-to-live for records in other servers' caches; 1-5 days are typical, and values of 3 or more days are recommended once the zone has stabilised. Individual records can override it, and the RFC suggests very large values, 1-2 weeks, for the MX, A and PTR records of mail hosts, the NS records of the zone and the A records of the nameservers.
sections.plainLanguage: The SOA record holds the contact address and the four timers that control how servers share and cache a zone. Use a date-based serial number, and choose timer values that match how often you change the data.

sections.title: Glue, Aliases, Mail and Wildcard Records
sections.content:
Glue records are the A records that accompany NS records so that a nameserver can bootstrap itself. They are required only in forward zone files, for nameservers inside the subdomain being delegated, and a multi-homed nameserver must list all of its addresses to avoid cache inconsistency caused by differing TTL values. Adding glue to every NS record by habit only makes things harder when a nameserver moves or is removed, and older versions of BIND could copy wrong glue into zone transfers and pass it on to other servers.

A CNAME record is an alias, and it cannot share its name with any other data. A zone that combines a CNAME with NS records is the classic mistake: BIND sees the alias, refuses to add other records for that name, and the NS entries are ignored, so every host in the zone disappears. The RFC also warns against records that point to other names, such as an MX pointing to a CNAME, because it adds needless indirection and makes servers work harder, and against chains of CNAMEs, which tickle bugs in some resolvers that fail to detect loops. NS records pointing to a CNAME are ignored by current BIND implementations, which can lead to a lame delegation.

Mail records have their own rules. Every host should have an MX record, even one that points to itself, because mail software always looks for an MX and a missing one costs an extra resolver query for every message. A wildcard MX applies only to names that are not in the zone at all, so it will not catch mail for a host that already exists. Wildcards are useful for sites whose hosts sit behind a firewall, where writing an MX for every host is impractical, and there the DNS is split into an internal part with explicit records and an external part with wildcards. The RFC also notes that WKS records are deprecated and should not be used, that HINFO needs both a hardware type and an operating system, and that TXT records are the right place for anything else.
sections.plainLanguage: Glue records, aliases, mail records and wildcards each have rules that are easy to break. An alias cannot share a name with any other record, a mail record should point at a real host, and a wildcard only covers names that are not in the zone at all.

sections.title: Delegation and Lame Nameservers
sections.content:
Every domain needs at least two nameservers, and more is preferred, with a secondary outside the site's own network. If a secondary is not under your control, check periodically that it is still receiving current zone data from you, and that queries to it about your hosts return an authoritative answer. A delegation that points at a server which does not actually answer for the zone is called a lame delegation. The classic case is a new domain whose second nameserver was never set up as a primary or secondary for it. The result is extra DNS traffic at best and unresolved hosts and bounced mail at worst.

A lame delegation also appears when a nameserver is moved or removed, because other sites still hold the old NS record in their caches. To prevent that, keep serving the zone from the old nameserver for as long as the maximum of the minimum and refresh times of the zone and of the parent zone. Sites that point at popular nameservers such as ns.uu.net in the hope of getting service make the problem worse by adding traffic to an already busy server.

The parent domain should carry the same NS records as the zone itself, including the in-addr.arpa zones. Do not list too many: 7 is the recommended maximum, and a longer list risks overflowing the 512-byte limit of a UDP response to an NS query, which makes resolvers fall back to TCP and adds load. Secondaries should be placed to keep latency low and to avoid depending on a single slow link.
sections.plainLanguage: A delegation tells the Internet which servers answer for a zone. If a delegated server does not answer, the delegation is lame, and lookups for that zone either fail or take extra traffic.

sections.title: Running the Nameserver Day to Day
sections.content:
Each zone carries a serial number that says who has the most current data, and a secondary asks the primary for a new copy only when the primary's serial number is greater. So every data change needs a new serial number, and automating the increment is a good idea. If a serial number was raised too high and has to be lowered, the RFC gives a procedure: add 2147483647 to the incorrect number, subtract 4294967296 if the result exceeds it, load the result, wait two refresh periods, and repeat until the number is below the target, then raise it to the target. This does not work with secondaries running BIND 4.8.3 or earlier.

Zone files should be written consistently, since a consistent style makes mistakes easier to spot. Use either fully qualified domain names everywhere or unqualified names everywhere, keep the columns lined up with tabs, keep the records for one host together, and remember the $ORIGIN: without a trailing dot a name is not fully qualified and the server appends the origin to it. Trailing dots matter most in in-addr.arpa zone files.

After any change, query the resolver with dig or another tool to confirm the data, and check the syslog output after reloading, because named reports grievous errors in the data or boot file there. Automating these checks, either before the files are loaded or against the data already in the server, is strongly recommended. The memo also lists zones that should always be present in a configuration, namely localhost, 0.0.127.in-addr.arpa, 255.in-addr.arpa and 0.in-addr.arpa, whose purpose is to answer for special addresses and to stop accidental queries for broadcast or local addresses from reaching the root servers. It closes with a note that security issues are not discussed in the memo, and a recommendation to turn on UDP checksums, which some Unix systems leave off to save processor cycles.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers only pick up new data when the serial number rises, so every edit needs a new serial number. Then check the result by querying the server, and keep the special local zones in place.
